title: Bounding an Integral using the Max-Min Inequality
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Show that 1 <= int_0^1 sqrt(1 + x^3) dx <= sqrt(2) using the Max-Min Inequality for definite integrals.

steps.title: Find Absolute Extrema on [0, 1]
steps.mathExpression: g(x) = \sqrt{1 + x^3} \text{ is strictly increasing on } [0, 1] \implies m = g(0) = 1, \quad M = g(1) = \sqrt{2}
steps.explanation: Since x^3 increases, the minimum occurs at x = 0 and maximum at x = 1.
steps.why: Extreme Value Theorem on closed intervals.

steps.title: Apply the Max-Min Inequality
steps.mathExpression: m(b - a) \le \int_a^b f(x) dx \le M(b - a) \implies 1(1 - 0) \le \int_0^1 \sqrt{1 + x^3} dx \le \sqrt{2}(1 - 0)
steps.explanation: Multiply minimum and maximum values by interval length 1.

steps.title: Conclude Bounds
steps.explanation: The integral is strictly bounded between 1 and sqrt(2).
